title: For firsts
hook: a blessing for new things, new seasons and first times each year
carry: you kept me alive for this

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating. Your line was full, then grateful.

The first strawberries of the summer. The first snow. The first time you hold a baby niece. The first night in a new apartment, eating takeout on the floor because the table hasn't arrived. A first can carry a quiet thought under the joy: I made it to this. Not everyone did. Some years it wasn't certain. Jewish tradition has a blessing for exactly that thought, short enough to say in a doorway. Today: Shehecheyanu.
screen: `THE FIRST STRAWBERRIES.` → `THE FIRST NIGHT IN A NEW PLACE.` → `I MADE IT TO THIS.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, the blessing says: shehecheyanu, v'kiyemanu, v'higianu lazman hazeh. Who has kept us alive, and sustained us, and brought us to this time. Three verbs. Kept us alive: you're still here. Sustained us: held up through everything in between. Brought us to this season: this exact moment. When is it said? The Talmud and later law list many moments. The first night of each festival, over the candles or the wine. The first lighting of the Hanukkah candles. A fruit eaten for the first time in its season: the first cherries, the first pomegranate of the year. Important new clothes, a new home, major new things you're glad of. A close friend you haven't seen in thirty days. And people say it at life's firsts: a baby's birth, a graduation, a wedding, the first time they do something they never thought they'd get to. Notice what the blessing isn't about. Not the strawberry being good, or the dress being nice. It's about time. There was a season when this was out of reach, and I've been carried here. Jewish law even allows saying it on just seeing a new fruit, because the joy is in the arrival, though the usual custom is to wait for the first bite. And on the second night of Rosh Hashanah, there's a custom of setting out a fruit not yet tasted that year, so the blessing has a clear reason to be said.
screen: `KEPT ALIVE, SUSTAINED, BROUGHT HERE.` · `FESTIVALS, FRUIT, NEW CLOTHES.` · `LIFE'S FIRSTS.` · `A BLESSING ABOUT TIME.` · then, large: `BROUGHT US TO THIS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Think back over this season and pick one first: the first cold morning, a first conversation, a first bite of something, a first day without pain, a first attempt at something. Remember when it was out of reach. If you pray, say the blessing, or just its English, who kept us alive and brought us to this time; if you don't, say it plainly: I made it to this.
Shehecheyanu. Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this time: the blessing for firsts and new seasons.
Your line: you kept me alive for this. A blessing about time, not things. Day one hundred sixteen, done.

howItsDone: Jews say Shehecheyanu on the first night of festivals, at the first Hanukkah candle, over a fruit's first eating in its season, over significant new clothes or a new home, and at many of life's firsts.
